style: former CBOT floor market maker, prop trader, now brokerage CEO; discretionary trend follower
edge_principles: Floor training taught only defense: a hard per-trade loss cap of a few ticks, with any larger loss requiring a written explanation; making money came from not losing it.
Only take trades where you can see a way out at breakeven or a tiny loss before you enter (enter where the odds favour a scratch).
Not trading (walking away for a day or a week) is a valid and often best decision.
Trade with the trend and relative strength; do not short strong names just because they look high or overvalued (most self-directed clients lose by fading moves).
Avoid opinion-heavy information (financial TV) before trading; react to price rather than predict.
Breaking your own rules is where large losses come from (his worst trade: a counter-trend gold short).
notes: Mostly career and life story (pits, brokerage founding, near-fatal illness). Two loosely specified ideas: the pit 'lean' scratch-scalp and buying sharp sell-offs inside strong uptrends.

edge_principles: Multiple-comparisons bias: every rule you screen is a test with a false-positive rate; test 1,000 ideas at 5% and about 50 will look good by chance. Count and report how many configurations were tried.
Overfitting: a model that fits history perfectly is also fitting noise; keep an untouched out-of-sample set and do not even explore it during development.
Re-using the holdout for idea after idea turns it back into in-sample data (multiple comparisons again); you get a limited number of holdout looks.
Non-stationarity: a time-split holdout can be a different regime; consider also splitting by asset (hold out a set of tickers) as an alternative holdout.
Survivorship bias: track records you hear about are the survivors of many random players; forward (out-of-sample) performance is the way to tell skill from luck.

Data-cleaning bias: vendor history is pre-corrected, so backtests never see the bad prints a live feed delivers; add live guards such as dropping or winsorizing prices more than ~3 standard deviations from the recent mean.
Diversify across many positions so a single bad print or idiosyncratic event cannot damage the book.
Alternative data edges (satellite car counts, oil tank shadows) decay once widely used.
notes: Statistics/methodology episode on biases; no trading setups. Directly supports MCF research rules (holdouts scored once, reporting number of configurations tried).

style: quant equity, cross-sectional factor research (Quantopian mini-series part 2)
edge_principles: Define the trading universe before researching: drop illiquid names, micro-caps, ETFs/leveraged ETFs and ADRs from a stock-ranking signal so ranked names are comparable and actually tradable at the modelled size.
Not doing universe selection at all is the most common mistake (e.g. a 5-day-return sort topped by a triple-levered ETF).
Apply a small edge to as many independent bets as capital allows; more positions lowers concentration risk and smooths returns, limited by per-trade fixed costs and share rounding on small accounts.
Rank a wide universe but trade only the extremes if capital is small; the further in from the edges, the smoother but weaker the returns.
Start from an economic hypothesis, then try hard to disprove it (rank correlation of the factor vs 1/5/10-day forward returns); most hypotheses fail.
A predictive factor can still lose money after costs; compare forecast edge per trade with round-trip cost before trading it.
Combine many weak, uncorrelated signals; individual signals are intermittent and regime-dependent.
Measure a strategy's exposure to known risk factors (market beta, size, momentum); returns that are mostly market beta add nothing and share its crash risk.
Faster participants trading the same signal can make a signal a reason not to trade (you would be behind them in the queue).
notes: Methodology episode on universe selection, alpha factors and risk factors. Two example factors (short interest, female CEO) are daily/position-horizon and need data MCF lacks.

style: quant equity, multi-factor combination (Quantopian mini-series part 3)
edge_principles: Single factors have decayed through competition; durable edges now come from combining many weak, low-correlation signals.
A signal only marginally better than 50% hit rate can still add value to a combined model if it is uncorrelated with the others.
With low correlation, returns add linearly while volatility grows roughly with the square root of the number of signals, so Sharpe rises; diminishing returns after about 25 equity factors.

Simple averaging of signals is a reasonable baseline; next step is weighting each signal by trailing (e.g. 3-month) accuracy; ML ensembles (boosting) help most at the combination step rather than for discovering signals.
Monitor factor decay by regressing a factor's returns on known factors and tracking the leftover alpha over time.
Keep the forecast horizon consistent across signals being combined.
A 55-60% hit rate is enough across hundreds of names, but a concentrated book of 10-50 names needs much higher accuracy for the same risk.
notes: Methodology episode on combining alpha factors (classifiers, ensembles, correlation). No concrete setups; relevant to how MCF could blend setup signals or weight them by recent hit rate.

style: quant portfolio construction / engineering (Quantopian mini-series part 4)
edge_principles: Treat portfolio construction as constrained optimisation: maximise forecast return subject to caps (e.g. max 1-5% per name), total leverage, market and sector neutrality, and limits on beta to known factors.
Remember you maximise estimated return; the forecast model can be wrong, so concentration in the single best forecast is rarely wise.
Hedge out market and sector moves when the hypothesis is relative ('these stocks beat similar stocks after event X'), otherwise a falling market can sink a correct thesis.

Check that a strategy is not secretly a sector or style bet (e.g. a fundamentals ranking that is really long tech) by regressing its returns on sector/factor return streams over a trailing window (~90 days).
Watch for look-ahead bias when building volatility/risk forecasts (misaligned windows that include the forecast period).
Returns are fat-tailed; value-at-risk computed under a normal assumption understates losses.
Naive Markowitz on historical means is implicitly a momentum bet and performs poorly; validate every implicit assumption.
Hybrid workflows are fine at low frequency: a human can flag an event and the systematic layer handles sizing and risk.
notes: Methodology episode on portfolio optimisation and risk constraints. One event-driven example (gun-maker stocks after mass shootings / gun-control news) needing a news/event feed.

style: quant data science / machine learning education (Quantopian mini-series part 5)
edge_principles: Direct ML price forecasting is the riskiest use: flexible models contort to price noise and fail out of sample; treat it as the last thing to try.
Better ML uses: turning unstructured data into scores (images, text), selecting a few variables from many, and combining existing signals.
Use ML to choose 2-5 candidate inputs, then fit a simple, explainable model and validate it like any other.
Prefer simple models with few parameters; required data grows rapidly with model complexity.
Avoid black-box models you cannot explain; you cannot tell whether good results come from a real driver.
When data are scarce use k-fold cross-validation and require consistent results across folds; inconsistent selected patterns mean you are fitting noise.
Once you look at the holdout it is no longer out-of-sample.
notes: Machine-learning methodology episode; no trading setups.

edge_principles: Before automating a discretionary desk, run factor/risk analysis on its existing return stream; it may just be leverage or known exposures.
Assume every strategy eventually loses its edge; monitor live performance with statistical process control (rolling Sharpe, drawdown, plus strategy-specific metrics).
Set live kill tolerances before deployment and obey them even when the strategy is still making money.
In multi-component strategies, monitor each component separately to catch a broken leg before the whole fails.
Model slippage per broker, market and time of day, and re-check it against live fills every couple of months.
Capacity: commissions limit small accounts, share of volume limits large ones; run the backtest at several capital levels and find where performance peaks.
Rule of thumb: an out-of-sample Sharpe above 1, or lower but very uncorrelated with known factors.
Common price-based technical signals are heavily commoditised; they may work through crowd behaviour but are prone to panics.
A model that works on only one instrument is a sample of one and suspicious of overfitting unless it came from a prior hypothesis; repeat the process on other instruments and diversify.
Too many portfolio constraints shows up as an optimiser with no solution or no trades; choose constraints by a process and keep them.
Factor interactions (e.g. mean reversion in large caps, momentum in small caps) are worth testing only from a hypothesis, because there are many possible interactions (multiple comparisons).
notes: Listener Q&A closing the Quantopian series; methodology and live-monitoring advice, no concrete setups.
Three-minute holiday greeting and community plug; no trading content.

edge_principles: Journaling reveals your real statistics and habits, including the ones you would rather not see.
In the intermediate stage progress shows up as earlier awareness of hesitation, forced trades and changing risk perception rather than in P&L; trading less can be part of that progress.
notes: Short solo end-of-2025 reflection on the 'middle' stage of trading; psychology only, no setups.

style: retail/prop-firm futures day trader; systematic-discretionary using proprietary ML key levels
markets: futures: NQ/ES/RTY/YM, gold/silver/copper/platinum, crude oil (RB, HO as reference)
edge_principles: Use levels fixed before the open (non-repainting); levels that adjust after the fact look perfect in backtests but cannot be traded.
Prefer precise single-price levels over wide zones; inside a zone you cannot tell a real break from a false one.
Filter level trades by cross-market agreement: require several correlated instruments to hit their levels at the same moment and none to contradict.
Optimise for lowest drawdown: time the entry rather than adjusting the stop; the stop is a catastrophe stop that should rarely be hit.
Take a level trade only when every correlated instrument has enough room to the next opposing level for at least 3:1 reward-to-risk.
Scale out when a correlated market reaches its opposing level, even before your own instrument reaches a target.
High-risk moments for rule-breaking: after a losing streak, after a long winning streak (first loss triggers oversizing), after missing an A+ setup.
Trading in front of others (live room) improved her rule adherence; accountability helps.

A coded backtest of a discretionary method is only an approximation and gives a lower bound on its performance; knowing the strategy's statistics makes a loss feel like part of the distribution rather than personal failure.
notes: Futures day trader trading synchronous reactions of correlated index (or metals) futures at precomputed key levels. Levels come from a proprietary model; the cross-asset confluence filter can be approximated in MCF with index ETFs and standard levels.

style: former COMEX copper pit scalper and HFT builder; now crypto derivatives fund CIO (Monarq)
markets: copper/energy futures, VIX futures (HFT), crypto options and perps
edge_principles: Pit-era edge came from pricing what others guessed at (copper strips/spreads) with a computer and then hedging the residual risk immediately; complex instruments are often mispriced.
HFT is the pit's scalping done faster and across many markets; structural edges migrate as market structure changes, so adapt or exit.
Early scalping: let stops get run, buy the last of the forced sellers, then exit quickly.
Predictable flows (index/fund futures rolls) are a repeatable event-driven edge.
Crypto options often underprice the fat right tail; when the volatility term structure inverts, longer-dated convexity can be cheaper than near-term.

Sentiment extremes (fear/greed index near lows, very low derivatives open interest, articles predicting zero) together with positive perp funding have marked past crypto washouts; one data point alone is not enough.
Markets can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent.
notes: Career and market-structure episode (COMEX, NYMEX technology, HFT, crypto). Setups are futures-roll and crypto-options ideas, loosely specified; nothing directly for intraday stocks.
